weeks.context: This week you are going to analyze Sample Superstore — the classic dataset every analyst learns on. It's 4 years of sales for a fictional retailer. By Sunday you'll have a 1-page Excel/Sheets dashboard plus a 1-page PDF memo answering 3 specific questions. If you have never used Excel formulas or pivot tables before, that is fine. items.title: Day in the life of a Data Analyst (12 min)
items.creator: various

items.title: The 3 questions
items.body:
By Sunday you'll answer these about Sample Superstore (a fake retailer):

Q1. Which sub-category (Phones? Chairs? Tables?) has the highest profit MARGIN? Which has the lowest?
Q2. Which region (West? East? Central? South?) grew sales the most year-over-year in the latest year?
Q3. Is Furniture overall a profitable category? Where does its profit come from?

Write your guess for each in guesses.txt. Check on Day 6.

items.title: Open and explore
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make the project folder.
  Make a folder on your Desktop called 'superstore-analysis'.

STEP 2 — Download the file from the card above. Move it into the folder.

STEP 3 — Open it.
  Right-click → Open with → Excel (or Google Sheets — upload via drive.google.com).

STEP 4 — Look at the sheets.
  YOU SHOULD SEE 3 sheets at the bottom: Orders, Returns, People.
  Click Orders. Scroll through. You see ~10,000 rows. Look at the columns: Order Date, Region, Segment, Category, Sub-Category, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

STEP 5 — Take a quick total.
  In a new cell anywhere: =SUM(Orders!N:N)
  (N is the Sales column — adjust the letter if yours is different.)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: about $2.3 million in total Sales. That's the size of the dataset.

Save the file. Done for today.

items.title: Drill the formulas
items.body:
Make a new sheet in the same workbook called 'Drills'.

STEP 1 — In A1 type 'Total sales 2023:', in B1 type:
      =SUMIFS(Orders!N:N, Orders!C:C, ">=2023-01-01", Orders!C:C, "<=2023-12-31")
  (Adjust column letters if yours are different. N=Sales, C=Order Date.)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: ~$700k.

STEP 2 — In A2 type 'Orders in West:', in B2 type:
      =COUNTIFS(Orders!I:I, "West")
  (I = Region column)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: ~3,000 orders.

STEP 3 — In A3 type 'Average discount:', in B3 type:
      =AVERAGE(Orders!O:O)
  (O = Discount)

STEP 4 — In A4 type 'XLOOKUP for customer CG-12520:', in B4 type:
      =XLOOKUP("CG-12520", Orders!E:E, Orders!F:F)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: that customer's name.

STEP 5 — In A5 type 'High-margin orders:', in B5 type a header. Then in row 6+ for the first 100 rows, add a new column 'Margin Bucket' next to Profit. Use:
      =IF(R2/N2 > 0.2, "Healthy", IF(R2/N2 > 0.05, "Thin", "Loss"))
  (R = Profit, N = Sales)

Save.

days.title: Pivot table for Q1 (margin leaders)

items.title: Pivot tables in 20 minutes — Leila Gharani

items.title: Build the margin pivot
items.body:
STEP 1 — Click anywhere in the Orders sheet.
  Insert → PivotTable → New worksheet → OK.

STEP 2 — Build the pivot.
  ROWS area: drag Sub-Category
  VALUES area: drag Sales (Sum), drag Profit (Sum)
  You should now see ~17 sub-categories with their Sales and Profit totals.

STEP 3 — Add Margin as a calculated field.
  PivotTable Analyze tab → Fields, Items, & Sets → Calculated Field.
  Name: Margin. Formula: = Profit / Sales
  Click OK.

STEP 4 — Format Margin as a percentage.
  Right-click any Margin number → Number Format → Percentage → 1 decimal → OK.

STEP 5 — Sort by Margin descending.
  Click the dropdown next to 'Sub-Category' → More Sort Options → Sort by Margin → Largest to Smallest.

STEP 6 — Write the answer to Q1.
  In a new cell: highest margin sub-category = ?
  Lowest margin sub-category = ?
  Save.

days.title: Pivot for Q2 (regional growth)
days.summary: Today: year-over-year growth by region.

items.title: Region YoY pivot
items.body:
STEP 1 — New pivot from Orders → new sheet.

STEP 2 — Build it.
  ROWS: Region
  COLUMNS: Order Date — Excel will offer to group by Year. Accept.
  VALUES: Sum of Sales
  You see a 4x4 table: each region's sales for each year.

STEP 3 — Add a YoY growth column.
  Outside the pivot (next column), for the latest year:
      = (Sales latest year - Sales previous year) / Sales previous year
  Format as percentage.

STEP 4 — Which region grew most? Write the answer to Q2 in a cell.

days.title: Pivot for Q3 (Furniture profitability)
days.summary: Is Furniture profitable? Drill in.

items.title: Furniture deep-dive
items.body:
STEP 1 — New pivot from Orders.
  Filter: Category = Furniture
  ROWS: Sub-Category
  VALUES: Sum of Profit

STEP 2 — Look at the result.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: Tables loses big money. Bookcases barely break even. Chairs make decent profit. Furnishings make the most.

STEP 3 — Add Region.
  Drag Region to COLUMNS.
  Now you see Furniture profit broken down by region AND sub-category.
  Which region is best for Furniture? Worst?

STEP 4 — Write the answer to Q3.
  Is Furniture overall profitable? (Add all the numbers — what's the total?)
  Where does the profit come from?

days.title: Build the dashboard + write the memo
days.summary: Today you ship.

items.title: Dashboard + Memo + Push
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make a new sheet called 'Dashboard'.

STEP 2 — Top row: 4 KPI cells.
  Total Sales: =SUM(Orders!N:N)
  Total Profit: =SUM(Orders!R:R)
  Profit Margin: =SUM(Orders!R:R) / SUM(Orders!N:N) (format as %)
  YoY Growth (latest year): use the formula from Day 5
  Style: make each cell big — font 20, bold, with a colored border.

STEP 3 — Middle: 2 charts.
  Chart 1: monthly sales trend (line). Source: a small pivot of Sales by month.
  Chart 2: sales by region (bar). Source: pivot of Sales by Region.

STEP 4 — Bottom: top 5 / bottom 5 sub-categories by margin (paste from Day 4 pivot).

STEP 5 — Write the memo.
  Open Word or Google Docs. Make a 1-page document. Use this exact structure:

      # Sample Superstore — Memo to leadership
      
      ## Headline
      (one sentence summarising everything)
      
      ## Q1. Margin leaders & laggards
      Highest margin: [name] at [%]
      Lowest margin: [name] at [%]
      Recommendation: [1 sentence — drop the laggard? double down on the leader?]
      
      ## Q2. Regional growth
      Fastest-growing region: [name] at [%] YoY
      Recommendation: [1 sentence]
      
      ## Q3. Furniture profitability
      Furniture total profit: $[X]
      Where the profit comes from: [Furnishings + Chairs mostly; Tables loses money]
      Recommendation: [1 sentence — discontinue Tables?]
      
      ## What I'd do next
      - [bullet 1]
      - [bullet 2]
      - [bullet 3]

  Export as PDF. Save as superstore-memo.pdf in the project folder.

STEP 6 — Push to GitHub.
  Open the 'create new repository' card. Name: superstore-analysis. Public.
  In your terminal:
      cd Desktop/superstore-analysis
      git init
      git add .
      git commit -m "Sample Superstore analysis v0.1"
      git branch -M main
      git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/superstore-analysis.git
      git push -u origin main

STEP 7 — Take a screenshot of the dashboard and add to README.

PASS CRITERIA — Superstore v0.1 ships when:
  ☐ Dashboard sheet with 4 KPIs + 2 charts + 1 table
  ☐ All 3 questions answered with specific numbers
  ☐ 1-page memo exported as PDF
  ☐ Public GitHub repo named superstore-analysis
  ☐ README has dashboard screenshot + link to memo PDF

items.title: Excel pain points
items.body:
Three things Excel does badly that pandas does well:
  1. >1M rows — Excel crashes; pandas yawns
  2. Repeating an analysis on next month's data — Excel: re-do; pandas: re-run
  3. Joining 5+ tables — Excel: VLOOKUP hell; pandas: 1 line

weeks.title: Superstore v0.4: SQL version
weeks.context: Everything you did in pivots can also be done in SQL — the language of every real database. Today you redo the same analysis in SQL.

items.title: SQLite Online — free in-browser SQL
items.why: Click 'Open' to use SQL right in your browser, no install.

items.title: Get Superstore into SQL
items.body:
Export the Orders sheet from Excel as 'orders.csv'.
In sqliteonline.com: Import → CSV → upload orders.csv → create table 'orders'.
Run: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
YOU SHOULD SEE: about 10,000 rows.

items.title: Margin leaders in SQL
items.body:
SELECT 
        "Sub-Category",
        SUM(Sales) AS total_sales,
        SUM(Profit) AS total_profit,
        SUM(Profit) * 1.0 / SUM(Sales) AS margin
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY "Sub-Category"
      ORDER BY margin DESC;

Save this query in queries.sql. Compare to your pivot — same answer?

items.title: Year-over-year in SQL
items.body:
SELECT 
        Region,
        strftime('%Y', "Order Date") AS year,
        SUM(Sales) AS total_sales
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY Region, year
      ORDER BY Region, year;

Compute YoY growth with a CTE:
      WITH yearly AS (
        SELECT Region, strftime('%Y', "Order Date") AS year, SUM(Sales) AS sales
        FROM orders GROUP BY Region, year
      )
      SELECT a.Region, a.year, a.sales,
             (a.sales - b.sales) * 1.0 / b.sales AS yoy_growth
      FROM yearly a
      LEFT JOIN yearly b ON a.Region = b.Region AND a.year = CAST(b.year AS INT) + 1
      ORDER BY a.Region, a.year;

items.title: Top 10 customers
items.body:
SELECT 
        "Customer ID", "Customer Name",
        SUM(Sales) AS lifetime_sales,
        SUM(Profit) AS lifetime_profit,
        COUNT(DISTINCT "Order ID") AS order_count
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY "Customer ID", "Customer Name"
      ORDER BY lifetime_sales DESC
      LIMIT 10;

weeks.title: Statistical thinking for analysts
weeks.context: Analysts who say 'this looks like a trend' but can't say 'p < 0.001' get pushed back by senior managers. This week — sampling, confidence intervals, correlation vs causation. Real-world traps you'll see daily.

items.title: Three biases
items.body:
When does Sample Superstore data MISLEAD?
  1. Only customers who already bought
  2. Only successful orders
  3. Only 4 regions, not all possible

items.title: CI for mean
items.body:
On Superstore data, pick 100 random orders:
      = AVERAGE(N2:N101) - 1.96 * STDEV(N2:N101) / SQRT(100)  (lower)
      = AVERAGE(N2:N101) + 1.96 * STDEV(N2:N101) / SQRT(100)  (upper)

Now pick 30 instead of 100. What happens to the CI? Why?

items.title: CORREL function
items.body:
=CORREL(Discount column, Profit column)

Result is between -1 and +1. What does -0.4 mean? -0.9? +0.1?
Now visualize as a scatter plot. Eyeball confirms?

items.title: Three spurious correlations in Superstore
items.body:
Pretend a junior analyst claims:
  1. 'Higher Discount causes lower Profit' (probably right but think...)
  2. 'Customer Segment = Corporate causes higher Sales' (right? wrong?)
  3. 'Region = West causes worse profit margin' (?)

For each, write what's REALLY happening + the confound.

items.title: T-test in Excel
items.body:
=T.TEST(consumer_sales_range, corporate_sales_range, 2, 3)

(2 = two-tailed, 3 = unequal variances)
Result: a p-value. If <0.05 the two segments have significantly different average sales.
Run for 3 region pairs. Document.

items.title: Find it
items.body: Pivot: Discount Bucket × Region → AVG Profit. Compare WITHIN one region vs OVERALL. Sometimes a trend in subgroups REVERSES when aggregated. Find one example in Superstore.

items.body:
pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas

Create scraper.py:
      import requests, time, pandas as pd
      from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
      headers = {'User-Agent':'forge-analyst scraper'}
      books = []
      for page in range(1, 6):
          url = f'https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-{page}.html'
          r = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
          soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
          for art in soup.select('article.product_pod'):
              title = art.select_one('h3 a').get('title')
              price = art.select_one('.price_color').text.replace('£','')
              books.append({'title': title, 'price': float(price)})
          time.sleep(1)
      pd.DataFrame(books).to_csv('books.csv', index=False)

weeks.title: A/B testing for product analysts
weeks.context: Product analyst roles ALWAYS ask: 'design an A/B test.' This week you do — applied to Olist. Test whether a 'free shipping over $50' rule lifts average order value. Compute lift, p-value, decision.

days.title: What product A/B tests look like

items.title: A/B testing in product analytics (15 min)
items.creator: various

items.title: Three real tests
items.body:
Product A/Bs you'd run at Olist:
  1. 'Free shipping over $50' (this week)
  2. 'Show product reviews above the fold'
  3. 'Send abandoned-cart email at 1hr vs 24hr'

items.title: Set up A and B groups
items.body:
From your Olist orders.csv: filter to delivered orders only.
Add a helper column: =IF(MOD(ROW(),2)=0, "A", "B") to randomly split.
Pretend the B group saw 'free shipping over $50' rule that boosted their order value by 8%. Add: =IF(group="B", payment_value * 1.08, payment_value) as 'order_value_in_test'.

items.title: Group A vs B
items.body:
Pivot: Rows = group (A/B), Values = AVG order_value_in_test, COUNT.
Compute lift: (B - A) / A.
Is it ~8%? Should be close (random noise will shift it slightly).

items.title: Test it
items.body:
=T.TEST(A_group_values, B_group_values, 2, 3)

Result < 0.05? Significant. Document.

items.title: How many do you need?
items.body:
Use evanmiller.org/ab-testing/sample-size.html or compute:
  Baseline mean: $150
  Minimum detectable lift: 3%
  Power: 80%
  Significance: 0.05
  → ~? users per arm

Document. This is exactly what product analysts compute weekly.

items.title: AB-PLAN.md
items.body:
# A/B Test — Free Shipping Threshold
      ## Hypothesis
  Free shipping over $50 increases AOV by ≥ 3%
      ## Setup
  - Random 50/50 split on new visitors
  - Run for 14 days
  - Primary metric: AOV
  - Secondary: conversion rate
      ## Sample size
  ~N per arm to detect 3% lift
      ## Decision criteria
  Ship if p<0.05 AND lift > 3%

weeks.title: Modern Data Stack — dbt + BigQuery
weeks.context: Big companies don't run SQL queries from notebooks. They use dbt — a tool that turns SQL into version-controlled, tested, reusable models. Plus BigQuery as the warehouse. This week you set both up (free tier) and rebuild your Superstore analysis as dbt models. Modern analyst skill, +$20k on your CV.

days.title: What is dbt and why do analysts use it
days.summary: Watch and understand. No setup yet.

items.title: Three problems dbt solves
items.body:
Write in notes.txt:
  1. 'I have 100 SQL queries in random files' — dbt makes them versioned + tested
  2. 'I copy-paste the same JOIN everywhere' — dbt lets you DEFINE a model once and reuse
  3. 'I don't know if my changes broke yesterday's reports' — dbt runs tests automatically

days.title: Set up BigQuery (free)
days.summary: Google's data warehouse. No credit card needed.

items.title: Google Cloud Console
items.why: Click 'Open'. Sign in with any Google account. Free tier includes $300 in credits and 1TB/month of BigQuery queries forever.

items.title: Create a BigQuery project
items.body:
STEP 1 — Sign in to console.cloud.google.com.

STEP 2 — Click the project dropdown (top, next to 'Google Cloud') → New Project.
  Name: forge-analytics. Click Create.

STEP 3 — Search 'BigQuery' in the top search bar. Open it.

STEP 4 — Run a free test query:
      SELECT 'Hello BigQuery' AS greeting;
  Click Run. YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Hello BigQuery' in 1 second.

days.title: Upload Superstore to BigQuery
days.summary: Your familiar data, now in the cloud.

items.title: Convert + upload
items.body:
STEP 1 — Convert your Superstore Excel to CSV.
  Open Sample - Superstore.xls. File → Save As → CSV. Save as orders.csv.

STEP 2 — In BigQuery, click the 3 dots next to your project name → Create dataset.
  Dataset ID: superstore. Location: US. Click Create.

STEP 3 — Click 3 dots next to your dataset → Create table.
  Source: Upload. File: orders.csv. Format: CSV. Table name: orders. Schema: Auto-detect. Create.
  Takes 10 seconds.

STEP 4 — Test:
      SELECT COUNT(*) FROM `forge-analytics.superstore.orders`;
  YOU SHOULD SEE: ~10000 rows.

days.title: Install dbt locally
days.summary: The tool itself, set up step by step.

items.title: Install dbt-bigquery
items.body:
STEP 1 — Open your terminal (Anaconda Prompt on Windows, Terminal on Mac).

STEP 2 — Install (this includes the BigQuery adapter):
      pip install dbt-bigquery
  Takes ~1 minute.

STEP 3 — Verify:
      dbt --version
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Core: 1.x.x  Plugins: bigquery 1.x.x'.

STEP 4 — Initialize a new dbt project:
      cd Desktop
      dbt init forge_analytics
  It asks: which adapter? Type 1 (BigQuery).
  Project name: forge_analytics. Method: oauth.
  Project ID: forge-analytics (the one from BigQuery).
  Dataset: superstore. Threads: 1. Location: US. Job execution timeout: 300.

STEP 5 — Verify the connection:
      cd forge_analytics
      dbt debug
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'All checks passed!'
  IF YOU SEE: 'authentication errors' — run 'gcloud auth application-default login' in a new tab, then retry.

days.title: Build your first dbt model
days.summary: SQL that's now tested + version-controlled.

items.title: Margin model
items.body:
STEP 1 — Open the forge_analytics folder in VS Code.
  Open models/example/. Delete the 2 sample files inside.

STEP 2 — Create a new file: models/example/sub_category_margin.sql
  Type:
      SELECT
        `Sub-Category` AS subcategory,
        SUM(Sales) AS total_sales,
        SUM(Profit) AS total_profit,
        SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(Profit), SUM(Sales)) AS margin
      FROM {{ source('superstore', 'orders') }}
      GROUP BY 1

STEP 3 — Tell dbt where the source is. Create models/example/sources.yml:
      version: 2
      sources:
        - name: superstore
          tables:
            - name: orders

STEP 4 — Run:
      dbt run
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Completed successfully' and a new table in BigQuery.

STEP 5 — Verify in BigQuery console:
      SELECT * FROM `forge-analytics.superstore.sub_category_margin` ORDER BY margin DESC LIMIT 5;
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 5 rows of top-margin sub-categories.

days.title: Add tests (docs OPTIONAL)
days.summary: Tests are required — that's what makes dbt powerful. Docs generation is great-to-see but optional this week.

items.title: Schema tests
items.body:
STEP 1 — Create models/example/schema.yml:
      version: 2
      models:
        - name: sub_category_margin
          description: 'Profit margin per sub-category'
          columns:
            - name: subcategory
              tests:
                - unique
                - not_null
            - name: margin
              description: 'Profit / Sales'

STEP 2 — Run the tests:
      dbt test
  YOU SHOULD SEE: '2 tests passed'.

STEP 3 — (OPTIONAL) Generate docs:
      dbt docs generate
      dbt docs serve
  Browser opens with a navigable diagram of your data + tests. This is what real analyst teams use.

days.title: Tag dbt-ready + commit
days.summary: Your modern stack project is shipped.

      ## Stack
      - Warehouse: BigQuery
      - Transformation: dbt

      - Tests: 2 passing (unique + not_null on subcategory)
      
      ## How to run
      pip install dbt-bigquery
      gcloud auth application-default login
      dbt run && dbt test

STEP 2 — Push:
      git init && git add . && git commit -m 'dbt v0.1: superstore on modern data stack'
      git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/superstore-dbt.git
      git push -u origin main

PASS:
  ☐ BigQuery project + dataset created
  ☐ Superstore data uploaded to BigQuery
  ☐ dbt installed + dbt debug passes
  ☐ At least 1 dbt model that runs successfully
  ☐ At least 2 tests passing
  ☐ (OPTIONAL) dbt docs generated locally
  ☐ Public GitHub repo named superstore-dbt

items.title: Pyramid principle
items.body:
Top: ONE clear answer.
Middle: 3 supporting findings.
Bottom: the data behind each.

This is how executives think — top-down. Build slides this way.

items.title: The headline
items.body:
Take your ForgeRetail Capstone. Write ONE sentence (≤ 20 words) that captures the most important thing you learned.

Examples:
  'Tables sub-category lost $X annually — exit or redesign within 90 days.'
  'Sales > $50k correlate with 3x repeat rate — invest in big-account onboarding.'

Hard. Iterate until it FITS on one slide.

items.title: Re-design slide 1
items.body:

  - Tell them what you told them (5 sec)
